name: Cryptic crossword No 26,333
preamble: Solutions to the five 'man' clues are of a kind, not further defined.

clue.text: Shortly to compete with notable college from Scandinavia

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase for a plural noun: Vikings are the people from Scandinavia

indicators.note: said shortly, a word is cut short, losing its final letter

blocks.note: VIE, to compete, without its last letter
King's College, Cambridge, one of the best-known colleges

explanation.surface: A famous college arranging a quick competition against visitors from Scandinavia.
explanation.walkthrough: King's College in Cambridge is famous enough to be the 'notable college'; the apostrophe is dropped in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norse seafaring raiders came out of Scandinavia, so the phrase describes them as a people.

clue.text: Release issued from the Royal Opera House?

indicators.note: what issues from something comes out of it, leaving part of the original behind

blocks.note: the Royal Opera House stands in Covent Garden, London, and the tail of COVENT is taken once the CO drops away

explanation.surface: A recording or announcement put out by the Royal Opera House.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Opera House is usually called simply Covent Garden after its London district; take the last four letters of COVENT.
explanation.definitionFit: To vent feelings or steam is to let them out, a straightforward synonym for releasing them.

clue.text: Man knows all the opening leads

indicators.note: the leads of a group are its front runners, so only the front letters count

blocks.note: the preamble's flag for a themed answer, which gives no letters
initials of these four words

explanation.surface: A man who knows every chess opening or bridge lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' only flags this as one of the preamble's five themed clues: each answer is a fictional manservant, never defined further.
explanation.definitionFit: Kato is the valet and chauffeur of the Green Hornet, so he fits the preamble's set of fictional manservants.

clue.text: Renewed life insurances rule out fliers — what a pain in the neck

indicators.note: ruling something out excludes it, so these letters are struck from the rest
something renewed is made over again, so the remaining letters are remade in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, letters to be removed

explanation.surface: Renewing life insurance policies that exclude cover for flying is a tiresome chore.
explanation.walkthrough: Strike F, L, I, E, R, S from LIFE INSURANCES to leave INSUANCE, then rearrange those eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for an annoying person or thing, which is exactly what a nuisance is.

clue.text: Declines to hear same time occurrences

indicators.note: what we hear is the spoken form, so the word is judged by its sound alone

blocks.note: syncs are things happening in synchronisation, at the same moment

explanation.surface: Someone turning down invitations because they clash with other events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Declines' reads as refuses; it is the verb for going down, as a ship or a value does.
explanation.definitionFit: When prices or fortunes go down they are said to fall or drop, the same sense as declining.

clue.text: Man in France I see regularly in Verviers

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other one, skipping in an even step

blocks.note: the preamble's flag for a themed answer, which gives no letters
the French word for I
second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of the Belgian town

explanation.surface: A tourist spotting a man in French-speaking Belgium at regular visits to Verviers.
explanation.walkthrough: Verviers is a town in French-speaking Belgium, which suits the French JE. 'Man' marks a themed clue: a fictional manservant, undefined.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeeves is Bertie Wooster's gentleman's gentleman in P G Wodehouse's stories, the most famous fictional valet.

clue.text: Next centre forward is a skilled performer

indicators.note: the centre is the middle, so only the inner letters are kept

blocks.note: the two middle letters
forward in the sense of cheeky or impudent

explanation.surface: A football manager naming the next centre forward as a skilful player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Centre forward' reads as one football position; split it, so 'centre' works on 'Next' and 'forward' means saucy.
explanation.definitionFit: An expert is someone highly skilled at a task, which a skilled performer is too.

clue.text: Controversial film cut you deviants out

indicators.note: a word cut short loses its tail
out can mean wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the word with its last letter cut
taken as written

explanation.surface: A censor telling deviant viewers that a contentious film has been cut.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1980s Britain a video nasty was a violent horror film on videotape that the press campaigned to ban.
explanation.definitionFit: These banned or prosecuted horror videos caused a moral panic, so a disputed film describes one.

clue.text: Stagger inside to get separate uniform

definitions.note: a verb phrase cluing an adjective: a split-level interior has staggered floors

blocks.note: to split is to separate
level means even or uniform

explanation.surface: A drunk staggering indoors to fetch a different uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stagger' suggests reeling, but here it means set at offset heights, as the floors of a house's interior can be.
explanation.definitionFit: A split-level building has rooms on floors raised half a storey apart, so its inside is staggered.

clue.text: Nourishment can be obtained from a ginger biscuit — tip off football team

indicators.note: with its tip taken off, a word loses its first letter

blocks.note: a ginger nut is a British ginger biscuit
Orient, as in Leyton Orient, a London football club, without its first letter

explanation.surface: Fans getting a snack at a match while the team is tipped off about something.
explanation.walkthrough: A ginger nut is a hard British ginger biscuit, and Leyton Orient is a London football club usually just called Orient.
explanation.definitionFit: A nutrient is a substance that feeds living things, so the word names a source of nourishment.

clue.text: A case most of all descriptive of snakes and eels

indicators.note: taking most of a word means keeping the greater part and dropping its tail

blocks.note: taken as written
a pod is a seed case
the word with its last letter gone

explanation.surface: A lawyer's case built on describing snakes and eels above all else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of all' reads as 'especially'; it is an instruction on the word 'all'.
explanation.definitionFit: Apodal is a zoological term for creatures lacking feet or limbs, which snakes and eels both are.

clue.text: His last car crash is jumped up

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter alone

blocks.note: the final letter
prang is British slang for a minor car crash

explanation.surface: A jumped-up driver's latest car smash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumped up' looks like the insult for an upstart, but it is simply leaped upwards; prang is British slang for a bump in a car.
explanation.definitionFit: To spring up is to leap upward, so the past tense matches having jumped up.

clue.text: Man is the key to everything

blocks.note: the preamble's flag for a themed answer, which gives no letters
surface reading: the secret that explains it all
setter's reading: a master key, the French name meaning it goes everywhere

explanation.walkthrough: Passepartout is Phileas Fogg's valet in Around the World in Eighty Days; his French name literally means 'passes everywhere' and also denotes a master key.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is also the French term for a master key that opens every lock in a building.

clue.text: Partner has recovered with a short drink

blocks.note: someone who has recovered is better
a half is half a pint of beer in a British pub

explanation.surface: A spouse back on their feet after illness, celebrating with a quick drink.
explanation.walkthrough: In a British pub a half is half a pint, the smaller measure of beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A jocular idiom for one's spouse, the person who shares your life as a partner.

clue.text: Withdrawal can be a topical relief

blocks.note: first meaning: pulling out of a race or contest
second meaning: easing an itch at the skin's surface

explanation.surface: Coming off a drug brings relief from an ointment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topical' suggests a skin cream; here relief applied to the surface is literal: rubbing an itch with your nails.
explanation.definitionFit: Horses and players are scratched from events when withdrawn, and scraping skin with fingernails soothes itching.

clue.text: Bishops can get this cycling endlessly about in back lane

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the word runs right to left
one thing set in another is held inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
cyclic means going round in repeating cycles without end

explanation.surface: Clergy cycling round and round a back lane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back lane' looks like an alley behind houses, but 'back' turns the word round and the cyclic piece sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An encyclical is a papal letter circulated to all the Catholic bishops, so it is something they receive.

clue.text: I'm having to live in the same place

indicators.note: to have something is to hold it, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: taken as written, the apostrophe dropped
to bide is to dwell or live somewhere

explanation.surface: Someone resigned to living at the same address.
explanation.walkthrough: Bide in the old sense of abide, to stay or dwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibidem is Latin used in footnotes, usually shortened to ibid, meaning the cited work is the same as before.

clue.text: One is back in intensive care

indicators.note: something inside other words sits within their letters
going back means reading in the opposite direction

blocks.note: the letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A patient is readmitted to intensive care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One is back' sounds like a returning patient; the letters sit across the words, read right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: In a pack of cards and on dice the single spot, the number one, is called the ace.

clue.text: Exhausted flower seller

blocks.note: a flower is something that flows, here a burn, Scottish for stream
a tout sells tickets, often unofficially

explanation.surface: A worn-out florist at the end of a long day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' wants to be a bloom; it is a thing that flows. A burn is a Scottish stream, and a tout sells tickets at inflated prices.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone burnt out has used up all their energy through overwork, an idiom for complete fatigue.

clue.text: Type of pot plant easily kept inside

indicators.note: what is kept inside is held within, so the letters lie within the words

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A houseplant in a pot that is easy to grow indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot plant' reads as one houseplant; split it, so 'pot' ends the definition and 'plant' starts the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: A teapot is a common kind of pot, so the word qualifies pot as its type.

clue.text: Cause displeasure when drugs let in another way

indicators.note: done another way means arranged differently from how it is given

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Smuggled narcotics slipping through another route upset the authorities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let in' looks like part of the story but is fodder too.
explanation.definitionFit: To disgruntle is to make someone discontented or annoyed, which is causing displeasure.

clue.text: Man confused brunette unendingly

indicators.note: with no ending, the word loses its final part
confused letters are muddled into a different order

blocks.note: the preamble's flag for a themed answer, which gives no letters
the word with its feminine -te ending removed

explanation.surface: A man left bewildered by a dark-haired woman, on and on.
explanation.walkthrough: Bunter is Lord Peter Wimsey's manservant in Dorothy L Sayers's detective novels; 'Man' marks him as one of the preamble's valets.
explanation.definitionFit: Mervyn Bunter serves Lord Peter Wimsey as valet, so he belongs to the preamble's class of fictional manservants.

clue.text: Earthy smell from refuse tips is re-emergent

indicators.note: the tips of something are its two ends, so only the outermost letters are kept

blocks.note: first and last letters
earthy humour is crude
a scent is a smell

explanation.surface: A rank odour rising again from rubbish dumps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse tips' reads as rubbish dumps; 'tips' instead takes the two ends of 'refuse', which go in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Recrudescent describes something breaking out again after a dormant period, as a disease may, so it is re-emerging.

clue.text: Decorative shell — getting one for nothing is a certainty

indicators.note: to get one thing for another is to swap it in place of the other

blocks.note: a conch is a large spiral seashell
the Roman numeral
zero, the letter shape

explanation.surface: Swapping an ornamental seashell for one that costs nothing is a sure thing.
explanation.walkthrough: The O of CONCH is swapped for I.
explanation.definitionFit: A cinch is informal for something sure or easy, so it names a certainty.

clue.text: Chinese fruit totally fails to get off the ground

definitions.text: totally fails to get off the ground

blocks.note: first meaning: the fruit once called the Chinese gooseberry

blocks.clueFragment: totally fails to get off the ground
blocks.note: second meaning: a flightless New Zealand bird

explanation.surface: An imported Chinese fruit product that flops completely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fails to get off the ground' reads as a flop; literally it is a bird that cannot fly. The second definition is a clause describing the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The kiwi fruit was sold as Chinese gooseberry, and the kiwi bird of New Zealand is entirely flightless.

clue.text: Celebrate a lot by the sound of it

indicators.note: judged by its sound means we listen to the word rather than read it

blocks.note: one's lot in life is one's fate

explanation.surface: Someone who seems to party a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot' reads as 'much'; it is one's lot, one's destiny.
explanation.definitionFit: To fete someone is to honour them with a celebration or lavish public praise.

clue.text: Fly first by way of the original Terminal One

indicators.note: the original version comes before any other, so the opening letter is taken
terminal means at the end, so only the final letter is taken

blocks.note: A is first, as in an A grade
via means by way of
the opening letter
the closing letter

explanation.surface: A passenger flying first class through the airport's first terminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terminal One' reads as an airport building; 'Terminal' instead takes the last letter of 'One', just as 'the original' takes the first of 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: To aviate is a formal verb for piloting or travelling in an aircraft, that is, to fly.

clue.text: One has got to mention mess up right away

indicators.note: to mess something up is to jumble it, so the letters come out in a new order

blocks.note: the Roman numeral
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone obliged to bring up a blunder immediately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mess up' looks like a noun, a blunder to mention; it is the instruction to jumble that word.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are idioms for immediately, without any delay at all.

clue.text: Man fails to open a giro transfer

indicators.note: what opens comes at the start, so the first letter is the one used
transferring letters moves them about into new positions

blocks.note: the preamble's flag for a themed answer, which gives no letters
the opening letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man unable to start a bank transfer.
explanation.walkthrough: A giro is a British bank transfer, so the surface reads as banking. Figaro is Count Almaviva's barber turned valet in Beaumarchais's plays and the operas of Rossini and Mozart.
explanation.definitionFit: Figaro becomes the Count's servant and valet in The Marriage of Figaro, fitting the preamble's manservants.

clue.text: Special link for mobile in hotel

indicators.note: something mobile moves about, so the letters change places

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A hotel offering a special connection for guests' mobile phones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' looks like a phone, which suits the hotel and the link; it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotline is a direct telephone connection reserved for urgent use, a dedicated communications channel.
